title: Associations of longitudinal BMI percentile classification patterns in early childhood with neighborhood-level social determinants of health.
ehr_evidence: We obtained patient-level EHR data from Nemours Children's Health - a large, multi-state pediatric health system in the US.
summary: In a longitudinal cohort of 36,910 children aged 0-7 years from a multi-state pediatric health system, data-driven and algorithmic clustering identified five BMI-percentile trajectory groups whose membership was significantly associated with neighborhood-level social determinants of health.
key_findings: Five BMI-percentile classification groups emerged: always having obesity (n=429; 1.16%), overweight most of the time (n=15,006; 40.65%), increasing BMI-percentile (n=9,060; 24.54%), decreasing BMI-percentile (n=5,058; 13.70%), and always normal weight (n=7,357; 19.89%).

Compared with the decreasing and always normal weight groups, children in the obesity, overweight, and increasing groups were more likely to live in neighborhoods with higher poverty, unemployment, crowded households, single-parent households, and lower preschool enrollment.
Multinomial logistic regression odds ratios for all 27 neighborhood SDOH variables had confidence intervals that did not cross 1, indicating all associations were statistically significant.
The 'increasing' group was associated with neighborhoods with higher Black population, higher unemployment, higher high-school dropout rates, and greater reliance on public assistance.

The 'decreasing' group was associated with neighborhoods with higher preschool enrollment and bachelor's education and lower poverty, public-assistance reliance, single-parent households, and crowded households.
population: 36,910 children aged 0-7 years from Nemours Children's Health, a multi-state pediatric health system spanning 5 US East Coast states
limitations: Patients were linked to a single census tract using their last available address, so relocations over time were not captured.
Selection bias may exist because children from lower-SES households may be more likely to move out of the health system.
Regional differences across states were not accounted for.
Potential interactions between the different SDOH variables were not analyzed.
